    Run clumppling

    gt_clumppling.Rd

    This function aligns multiple runs of a clustering algorithm (e.g. ADMIXTURE or STRUCTURE) with the method of clumppling (Liu, Kopelman and Rosenberg 2024). gt_clumppling() is anative R and C++ code port, with modifications to enhance performance, from the python package clumppling (version 2.0.10, by Xiran Liu; https://github.com/PopGenClustering/Clumppling), and gives the same results without the need for Python. The main modifications are that the alignment of each pair of runs, an integer linear program in clumppling, is solved exactly as an equivalent assignment problem, and that community detection uses ports of the implementations that clumppling uses through cdlib (python-louvain, in C++, and markov_clustering, in R) or the igraph package. If you use this function, make sure that you cite the paper on clumppling by Liu, Kopelman, and Rosenberg (2024).

    gt_clumppling(
  x,
  use_rep = TRUE,
  merge = TRUE,
  cd_method = "louvain",
  use_best_pair = TRUE,
  seed = NULL,
  output_path = NULL,
  cd_res = 1,
  test_comm = FALSE,
  comm_min = 1e-06,
  comm_max = 0.01
)

    Arguments

    x

    a gt_admix object with at least two Q matrices

    use_rep

    boolean, whether to use representative modes (alternative: average), defaults to TRUE

    merge

    boolean, whether to merge two clusters when aligning K+1 to K, defaults to TRUE

    cd_method

    the community detection method to use, one of 'louvain' (default), 'leiden', 'infomap', 'markov_clustering', 'label_propagation', 'walktrap', 'custom'. 'leiden', 'infomap', 'label_propagation' and 'walktrap' require the 'igraph' package; as in clumppling (which calls them through 'cdlib'), only 'louvain', 'infomap' and 'markov_clustering' use the similarity between replicates as edge weights, while 'leiden', 'label_propagation' and 'walktrap' only use the presence of edges (all pairs of replicates are connected, except for the most dissimilar pair). 'custom' reproduces the example custom method of clumppling (Markov clustering with a pruning threshold of 0.2); alternatively, cd_method can be a function that takes the adjacency matrix between replicates (similarities rescaled to [0, 1], with ones on the diagonal) and returns a vector of community labels.

    use_best_pair

    boolean, whether to use best pair as anchor for across-K alignment (alternative: major), defaults to TRUE

    seed

    (optional) an integer used to set the random seed, so that community detection (e.g. 'louvain') is reproducible. Defaults to NULL (no seed is set).

    output_path

    deprecated and ignored. Results are returned as R objects rather than written to files.

    cd_res

    the resolution of the 'louvain' community detection method, defaults to 1

    test_comm

    boolean, whether to test for community structure (with a Tracy-Widom test) before running community detection; if there is no structure, all replicates form a single mode. Defaults to FALSE.

    comm_min, comm_max

    cost thresholds for community detection: if all pairwise costs between replicates are below comm_min, they form a single mode; if they are all above comm_max, each replicate is a mode. Defaults to 1e-6 and 1e-2.

    Value

    a list of class gt_clumppling containing:

    • aligned_modes: a list of data.frames, each data.frame is a Q-matrix

    • cost_acrossK: a named list of costs for each pairwise K alignment

    • mode_replicates: a list of replicate indices for each mode

    • K_range: vector of K values analyzed

    • N: number of individuals

    • mode_stats: a data.frame with the size, cost and performance (average similarity among replicates) of each mode

    Details

    The example data (capeverde_admix.rds and chicken_admix.rds in extdata) are the example datasets of clumppling: runs of ADMIXTURE on the Cape Verde data of Verdu et al. (2017), and runs of STRUCTURE on the chicken data of Rosenberg et al. (2001).

    The algorithm has three steps:

    1. all pairs of replicates with the same K are aligned, finding the matching of clusters that minimises the squared distance between their memberships;

    2. replicates with the same K are grouped into modes by community detection on the network of alignment costs; each mode is summarised by a representative replicate (the one with the smallest cost to the others) or by the average of its replicates;

    3. modes are aligned across K (merging two clusters of the larger K when two values of K differ by one), and their clusters are reordered so that they are consistent across K.

    The replicates are the Q matrices of a gt_admix object, as returned by the clustering functions of 'tidypopgen' (e.g. tidypopgen::gt_admixture()) and 'tidygenclust' (e.g. gt_radmix()); to align replicates stored as Q files, read them into a gt_admix object with tidypopgen::read_q_files(). Replicates with the same K are numbered in the order in which they appear in the gt_admix object. The rows of each Q matrix must sum to 1 (to within 1e-6), so memberships that were rounded (e.g. by STRUCTURE) should be rescaled first.

    If you would like to generate an annotated autoplot from your gt_clumppling object, ensure that all individuals from the same population are adjacent to one another in the gt_admix object supplied to gt_clumppling (see tidypopgen::gt_admix_reorder_q()). Autoplot 'group' argument requires that all individuals from the same group are adjacent.

    The only random step is community detection. For the default 'louvain' method, the C++ implementation follows python-louvain (used by clumppling), but random numbers are drawn from R's generator: the modes are the same as in python unless the community structure is ambiguous, but the same seed does not give the same random choices in R and python. If seed is given, the state of R's random number generator is restored on exit. When a mode includes replicates with identical Q matrices, the representative of the mode can also differ from the python implementation (it is then an identical replicate), as their costs only differ by rounding errors.

    References

    X. Liu, N. M. Kopelman, N. A. Rosenberg (2024) Clumppling: cluster matching and permutation program with integer linear programming. Bioinformatics 40(1): btad751. doi: https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btad751

    N. A. Rosenberg, T. Burke, K. Elo, M. W. Feldman, P. J. Freidlin, M. A. M. Groenen, J. Hillel, A. Mäki-Tanila, M. Tixier-Boichard, A. Vignal, K. Wimmers, S. Weigend (2001) Empirical evaluation of genetic clustering methods using multilocus genotypes from 20 chicken breeds. Genetics 159(2): 699-713.

    P. Verdu, E. M. Jewett, T. J. Pemberton, N. A. Rosenberg, M. Baptista (2017) Parallel trajectories of genetic and linguistic admixture in a genetically admixed creole population. Current Biology 27(16): 2529-2535.

    Examples

    capeverde <- readRDS(
  system.file("extdata", "capeverde_admix.rds", package = "tidygenclust")
)
clump_res <- gt_clumppling(capeverde, seed = 1)
clump_res$mode_stats
#>   Mode Representative Size         Cost Performance
#> 1 K2M1       39_K2R39   50 8.043783e-14   0.9999998
#> 2 K3M1       65_K3R15   50 3.067899e-09   0.9999592
#> 3 K4M1      112_K4R12   39 7.341008e-04   0.9788892
#> 4 K4M2      138_K4R38   11 4.944349e-02   0.7918295
#> 5 K5M1      192_K5R42   18 5.074185e-02   0.7939366
#> 6 K5M2      167_K5R17   18 3.704965e-02   0.8188414
#> 7 K5M3      160_K5R10   14 2.550706e-02   0.8478811
